prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms held at a magic wavelength allow frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep the optical lattice clock (B052) as the sole part, with Katori and Ye. Round 1 did not turn up any objection to the physics: all eight members name it, nobody disputes that the magic-wavelength condition cancels the light shift, that Lamb-Dicke confinement removes Doppler and recoil shifts, that many atoms are interrogated in parallel, or that about 1e-18 has been reproduced in independent laboratories and on several species. The chair's first question asks what separates this from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. My answer is that those prizes honoured a way to count optical cycles and the control of single trapped quantum systems, while the lattice clock is a different mechanism: a large ensemble of neutral atoms, each in a state-insensitive trap, so that statistical power and systematic control come together. That is also why it directly tests relativity at millimetre scales, constants and dark-matter couplings. A citation that names the magic-wavelength lattice and the 1e-18 demonstrations, and does not mention the future definition of the second, states what was shown. Katori proposed and first realised the scheme and Ye's group took it to the lowest uncertainty, which gives a two-name credit that follows the intellectual history. As an experimentalist I use one test: what has been measured and by whom. This candidate passes it with the least attribution risk on the shortlist. My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is the one Eriksson and Mehlig raise: the clock is a superb instrument and a precision advance in a lineage the committee has honoured twice, and it may look incremental beside a new class of matter (B021) or a new class of many-body experiments (B044). I do not think it is incremental in mechanism, but the force of the objection depends on citation wording, so I would insist on the lattice scheme and not on 'optical clocks'. Second, PTB, SYRTE, NIST, and Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemke, Hinkley and Bloom built and improved the strontium and ytterbium platforms, so a two-name credit draws a narrow line that I cannot verify from the supplied record; priority dates are from memory. Third, the redefinition of the second has not happened, and Eriksson and Olsson treat that as a timing argument. I regard it as an argument about the metrological application, not about the confirmed physics. Fourth, my own preferred opening candidate, the Higgs discovery (B010), has more scientific weight than any other shortlisted item, but round 1 did not produce a defensible three-name credit and I will not argue otherwise.

responses.point: Mehlig explains that he ranked B052 seventh for the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and the pending redefinition, has since moved it up to his first alternative, and prefers B044 for its qualitatively new class of many-body experiments, while accepting B052 if the committee values attribution certainty.
responses.response: This answers the question I asked in round 1, and I am relieved that it is overlap and timing and not a hidden flaw in the systematics. On overlap, I would put it this way: a comb counts optical cycles and a trapped ion is one controlled quantum system, but a magic-wavelength lattice holds thousands of atoms at once without perturbing the transition, which is a new experimental regime. On B044 I accept your argument that the theory-plus-experiment story is coherent and the physics mature. My difficulty remains the third place. You settle it with Zoller, I proposed Esslinger, and neither of us can show from the supplied record that the other is wrong, while Zoller also stands on B009. A prize that must choose between those names without evidence I would rather not award this year. If you can accept B052 on the condition that the citation names the lattice scheme, I think we agree on more than the ballots suggest.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect (B021), says the clock is an incremental advance in a field already honoured, but would accept B052 without objection if clean credit is preferred; he also suggests narrowing the B021 citation to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant.
responses.response: I take the narrowed B021 citation seriously, and a new class of electronic matter is a larger conceptual step in the way you describe. But I do not think a narrower citation removes the problem. The first experiment in HgTe followed a specific prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and two other members, Mehlig and Olsson, agree that the experimental half cannot be stated honestly without that credit. The 2016 prize also makes closeness an issue that I cannot judge as well as you can. For the clock I would say the reverse: where your concern is incrementalism and mine is attribution, the lattice-scheme citation addresses yours and the two names address mine. I am glad you would accept B052, and I note that you rank it ahead of your other alternative.

responses.point: Olsson argues that B011 satisfies the criterion of a measurement-enabling advance at least as well as B052, that the pending redefinition applies to the clock and not to an instrument already in use for twenty years, and that B052 is nevertheless a strong consensus candidate.
responses.response: I accept that the corrector credit for Rose, Haider and Urban maps onto what each did, and that is a real advantage over B010, where I agree with you. I still think the clock wins on two points. First, the clock result is a direct test of physics and not only a tool: it measures gravitational redshift across millimetres and sets limits on varying constants. Second, the corrector lineage splits between TEM and STEM, and a three-name list cannot cover both, which is a gap in attribution of the kind I am trying to avoid. On timing, I agree the redefinition is not a good reason to wait for the clock, since the physics is confirmed without any SI decision. I do not think the clock is the only possible prize, but I do not see enough from round 1 to rank B011 above it, and I would be glad to see it considered in another year.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock tests physics and is not only a tool, that the credit goes naturally to Katori and Ye, and asks whether his research stay in John Hall's laboratory, where Ye trained, requires disclosure or recusal for B052.
responses.response: I agree on the physics. On your question, I would treat the stay as a disclosure and not a recusal: it involved no co-authorship with Katori or Ye and no other tie is recorded, and the chair of this committee has no standing to ask for more without a documented relationship. I would record it in the minutes and let you vote. I would, however, give your technical views on the 1e-18 systematics more weight than mine, since your area is closer to the work.

uncertainties: Whether the committee should wait for a formal redefinition of the second, or whether confirmed performance at 1e-18 is enough; I think it is enough, but Eriksson and Olsson do not agree.
Whether Katori and Ye are the right two names given the work of PTB, SYRTE, NIST and the Tokyo and JILA groups; I recall priority dates from memory and have not verified them.
Whether a citation tied to the magic-wavelength lattice will persuade Eriksson and Mehlig that the clock is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or whether they will still see an increment.
Whether a two-part prize is possible: B052 together with any other candidate would exceed three people unless a credit were split, and I would not split one.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B052; no tie to Katori, Ye or any lattice-clock group is recorded. My background in CERN-based particle physics and in cosmic-ray and gamma-ray instruments (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGO+) is close to the subject of my alternatives B010 and B043, but no personal tie to any credited person is recorded, so I recuse myself from none of them. I note Kroll's disclosure on B052 and do not consider it disqualifying.
